title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 6.3.1 Grammar in Use: Word Classes (Quantifiers)

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Quantifiers are words that tell us how much or how many. In this sub-strand you will sort countable and uncountable nouns, then use many, much, some and any in sentences about messages, time and information on the internet.

## Strand 6.0: Internet - Email
Sub-strand 6.3.1: Grammar in Use: Word Classes (Quantifiers)
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify quantifiers and nouns used with them appropriately for effective communication
b) use quantifiers in sentences correctly for communication clarity
c) adopt the correct use of quantifiers in everyday communication

## What this sub-strand covers
• Quantifiers

## Key inquiry questions
1. How can we quantify nouns we cannot count?

## Core competencies
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: This is enhanced as the learner composes poems and paragraphs using own ideas.
• Digital Literacy is manifested as the learners manipulates digital devices while downloading and composing poems.

## Values
• Unity: This is promoted as the learner is able to cooperate with peers as they recite poems and role-play dialogues.
• Love: This is developed as the learner demonstrates care to peers when assisting them to recite a poem.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Citizenship: Social cohesion is enhanced as the learner harmoniously interacts and use quantifiers in sentences during group tasks.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to relate the concept of quantifiers to their learning in Mathematics.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 6.0 Internet-Email, Sub-strand 6.3.1 Word Class: Quantifiers

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Countable and uncountable nouns

LESSON 1: COUNTABLE AND UNCOUNTABLE NOUNS
=========================================

## What you will learn
• Decide whether a noun can be counted one by one.
• Use a or a number only with countable nouns.
• Name which quantifiers are likely to follow each kind of noun.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify quantifiers and nouns used with them appropriately for effective communication

## Introduction
You can count emails: one email, two emails, many emails. You do not say one information or two informations. Before you choose much or many, you have to know what kind of noun you have.

## Notes
### Countable nouns
A countable noun has a singular and a plural. You can put a number in front of it, or a or an when it is singular.

- one computer, two computers
- a message, many messages
- a keyboard, three keyboards
- a picture, some pictures
- a phone, any phones

### Uncountable nouns
An uncountable noun names something we treat as a mass or an idea. In ordinary sentences it has no plural with s, and we do not use a or a number directly in front of it.

- information, not informations
- time, when we mean an amount of time
- water, rice, sugar, bread
- advice, homework, money
- air

We can measure these with another phrase: a piece of information, a glass of water, an hour of time, a bag of rice. The noun after of stays uncountable.

### A mixed list from the theme
Countable: emails, computers, links, keyboards, pictures, passwords (each secret word is one password), replies.
Uncountable: information, time, advice, money, internet traffic is too technical. Say information on the internet.

Email can be countable when you mean separate messages: three emails. It can be uncountable when you mean the activity: I sent email this morning. At Grade 4, if you can say three of them, treat them as countable: many emails.

### Why the sort comes first
Many is for plural countable nouns. Much is for uncountable nouns. Some and any can work with both, which you will practise next. If you sort the noun wrongly, the quantifier will sound wrong too: much keyboards, many informations.

Water and rice belong in this lesson so the pattern is clear, even though the stories around them may be about a computer lab. 'There is some water in the jug' and 'There are some computers on the desk' use different verbs, is and are, for the same reason.

## Key words
• quantifier — a word such as many, much, some or any that tells how much or how many
• countable noun — a noun you can count, with a singular and a plural, such as message and messages
• uncountable noun — a noun you do not count one by one, such as information, water or time

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Is 'advice' countable or uncountable?

Working:
1. Try a number in front of it.
2. We do not say two advices. We say some advice or a piece of advice.

Answer: Uncountable

### Example 2
Sort these words: keyboard, information, email messages, sugar.

Working:
1. Keyboards and messages can be counted.
2. Information and sugar cannot be counted one by one in ordinary speech.

Answer: Countable: keyboard, email messages. Uncountable: information, sugar.

## Activity: Sort the teacher's list
You will need: A list of nouns on the board: computer, water, message, rice, picture, advice, keyboard, time, email, homework, link, money
1. Copy the list into two columns: countable and uncountable.
2. For each countable noun, write the plural.
3. For each uncountable noun, write a measuring phrase such as a piece of or a glass of where it fits.
4. Compare columns with another group and correct any word that changed columns.

## Practice
1. Which sentence is correct: 'an information' or 'a piece of information'?
2. Write the plural of keyboard and of link.
3. Why is 'many sugars' wrong when you mean an amount of sugar in tea?
4. Name two countable nouns and two uncountable nouns from the lesson.

## Summary
• Countable nouns can take a number and a plural.
• Uncountable nouns such as information and water do not.
• Sort the noun before you choose many or much.

### Answers to practice
1. a piece of information
2. keyboards; links
3. Sugar is uncountable in that sense. Say some sugar or a little sugar, not many sugars.
4. Countable examples: emails, computers, pictures, keyboards. Uncountable examples: information, time, water, advice.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Many and much

LESSON 2: MANY AND MUCH
=======================

## What you will learn
• Use many with plural countable nouns.
• Use much with uncountable nouns.
• Ask questions with How many and How much.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify quantifiers and nouns used with them appropriately for effective communication; b) use quantifiers in sentences correctly for communication clarity

## Introduction
How many computers are in the lab? How much time do we have? The noun at the end of each question has already chosen the quantifier. Swapping them makes the question hard to answer.

## Notes
### The pair
Many goes with plural countable nouns.

- many emails
- many pictures
- many learners
- How many messages are in the inbox?

Much goes with uncountable nouns.

- much information
- much time
- much advice
- How much time is left?

Notice the verb. Plural countable nouns take are: There are many computers. Uncountable nouns take is: There is much information. In questions and negative sentences, much is especially common: We do not have much time. Is there much rice? In a positive sentence, people often say a lot of, but much is still correct in school sentences such as 'The page gave me much information.'

### Not every large amount uses many
There are many links on the page. There is much information behind one link. The links can be counted. The information is treated as a mass.

Money is uncountable: much money, not many money. Coins and notes can be counted if you mean the objects: many coins.

### A rhyme to keep the pair
How many emails?
Count them one by one.
How much information?
Much, when the reading is done.
Many phones, many pictures,
sitting in a line.
Much time, much water,
much advice of mine.

Say phones and pictures with many because you can count them. Say time, water and advice with much because you cannot.

### Building a sentence
Choose the noun, decide if you can count it, then pick many or much. Add a verb that matches.

- There are many keyboards, but there is not much space on the desk.
- How many replies did we send, and how much help did we need?

## Key words
• many — a quantifier used with plural countable nouns
• much — a quantifier used with uncountable nouns
• plural — the form of a noun that means more than one

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Choose many or much: How ____ pictures did you save?

Working:
1. Pictures are countable and plural.
2. Use many.

Answer: How many pictures did you save?

### Example 2
Choose many or much: We do not have ____ time.

Working:
1. Time, meaning an amount, is uncountable.
2. Use much, especially in a negative sentence.

Answer: We do not have much time.

## Activity: Fill the blanks in the rhyme
You will need: The rhyme written with blank spaces before emails, information, phones and time, Slates
1. In small groups, recite the rhyme and clap on many and much.
2. Fill four blanks the teacher has erased. Say whether the noun is countable or uncountable before you choose.
3. Write two How many questions and two How much questions about the computer lab.
4. Ask them across the group and answer in full sentences.

## Practice
1. Complete: There are ____ computers and not ____ space.
2. Which question is correct: 'How many information?' or 'How much information?'
3. Why do we say many coins but much money?
4. Write a sentence using many and the noun messages.

## Summary
• Many goes with plural countable nouns.
• Much goes with uncountable nouns.
• How many and How much follow the same rule.

### Answers to practice
1. There are many computers and not much space.
2. How much information?
3. Coins can be counted one by one. Money, as an amount, is uncountable.
4. There are many messages in the inbox. Any correct sentence is acceptable.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Some and any

LESSON 3: SOME AND ANY
======================

## What you will learn
• Use some in positive sentences.
• Use any in questions and negative sentences.
• Use some and any with both countable and uncountable nouns.

Curriculum outcomes: b) use quantifiers in sentences correctly for communication clarity; c) adopt the correct use of quantifiers in everyday communication

## Introduction
Some and any do not care whether the noun is countable or uncountable. They care about the kind of sentence. A positive sentence welcomes some. A question or a negative sentence usually prefers any.

## Notes
### The usual pattern
Some means a number or an amount when we are not being exact. It is normal in positive sentences.

- I have some messages. (countable)
- There is some information on the page. (uncountable)
- We saved some pictures.

Any is normal in questions and in sentences with not.

- Are there any messages?
- Is there any information?
- We do not have any paper.
- There are not any strange links from people we know.

Both quantifiers work with plural countable nouns and with uncountable nouns. Do not use them with a singular countable noun. Say a computer, not some computer, when you mean one. Some computers is correct because computers is plural.

### Two honest exceptions
Offers and requests often use some, even though they are questions: Would you like some water? Please give me some help.

Any can mean 'it does not matter which' in a positive sentence: Press any key. Click any picture your teacher has approved. This any does not mean 'none'.

Learn the usual pattern first. Add the exceptions when you meet them, so you do not 'correct' a polite offer into something stiff.

### A short poem
Some emails are friendly.
Some time is left today.
Are there any dangers?
We do not open any strange links that come our way.
If we need some advice,
we ask an adult to stay.

### Speaking in a dialogue
Amina: Have we any replies?
Baraka: We have some replies from the teacher. We do not have any replies from strangers.
Amina: Good. I have some time. Let us read the known messages.

Use the quantifiers in real talk about the lab, the kitchen or the classroom. The rule is the same for emails and for rice: some in the positive, any in the question and the negative.

## Key words
• some — a quantifier used for an unspecified amount, usually in positive sentences
• any — a quantifier usually used in questions and negative sentences
• positive sentence — a sentence that states something is so, without not
• negative sentence — a sentence that uses not or another negative word

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Choose some or any: There are ____ pictures in the folder.

Working:
1. The sentence is positive.
2. Use some.

Answer: There are some pictures in the folder.

### Example 2
Choose some or any: Did you find ____ information?

Working:
1. The sentence is a question.
2. Use any with the uncountable noun.

Answer: Did you find any information?

### Example 3
Why is 'Would you like any water?' less natural as an offer than 'Would you like some water?'

Working:
1. Offers are an exception.
2. Some sounds like a real offer. Any in a question can sound as if you expect the answer no.

Answer: Offers usually take some.

## Activity: Quantifiers in a role-play
You will need: The poem, Cards labelled some, any, many, much
1. Recite the poem in a small group until the some and any lines are easy.
2. Fill three blanks the teacher gives you: a positive sentence, a question and a negative sentence.
3. Role-play a short dialogue in the computer lab using some and any at least once each.
4. If a device is free, type one verse of your own that includes the four quantifiers. Do not search unknown websites.

## Practice
1. Fill in: We have ____ paper, but we do not have ____ ink.
2. Make a question with any and the noun messages.
3. Which offer is the natural one: 'Would you like some help?' or 'Would you like any help?' when you warmly mean it?
4. Can some be used with an uncountable noun? Give an example.

## Summary
• Some is usual in positive sentences. Any is usual in questions and negatives.
• Both can be used with plural countable nouns and with uncountable nouns.
• Offers often use some. 'Any key' can mean one of all the keys.

### Answers to practice
1. We have some paper, but we do not have any ink.
2. Are there any messages? Any correct question is acceptable.
3. Would you like some help?
4. Yes. There is some information on the page.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 6.3.1 GRAMMAR IN USE: WORD CLASSES (QUANTIFIERS)
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which noun is uncountable?
   A. keyboard
   B. message
   C. information
   D. picture

2. Which noun is countable?
   A. rice
   B. advice
   C. email messages
   D. water

3. Choose the correct phrase.
   A. many informations
   B. much information
   C. a information
   D. two advices

4. How ____ computers are in the lab?
   A. much
   B. many
   C. a
   D. information

5. We do not have ____ time.
   A. many
   B. much
   C. a
   D. several time

6. There are ____ pictures in this folder. The sentence is positive.
   A. any
   B. some
   C. much
   D. a

7. Are there ____ replies from the teacher?
   A. some
   B. any
   C. much
   D. a

8. Which sentence is a natural offer?
   A. Would you like some water?
   B. Would you like many water?
   C. Would you like a water?
   D. Would you like much waters?

9. 'Press any key' means
   A. press none of the keys
   B. press one key, and it does not matter which approved key
   C. press much key
   D. delete the keyboard

10. Write a negative sentence using any and the noun links.
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 6.3.1 GRAMMAR IN USE: WORD CLASSES (QUANTIFIERS)
========================================

1. C. information
   We say a piece of information, not two informations.

2. C. email messages
   Messages can be counted: one message, two messages.

3. B. much information
   Information is uncountable, so it takes much.

4. B. many
   Computers are plural and countable.

5. B. much
   Time as an amount is uncountable and the sentence is negative, so much fits.

6. B. some
   Some is used in a positive sentence with a plural noun. A would need a singular noun.

7. B. any
   Questions usually take any.

8. A. Would you like some water?
   Offers use some, and water is uncountable.

9. B. press one key, and it does not matter which approved key
   In this positive sentence, any means one out of the set.

10. We do not click any strange links.
   Any belongs in the negative sentence, and links is a plural countable noun.

4. If a device is free, type one verse of your own that includes the four quantifiers. Do not search unknown websites.

## Practice
1. Fill in: We have ____ paper, but we do not have ____ ink.
2. Make a question with any and the noun messages.
3. Which offer is the natural one: 'Would you like some help?' or 'Would you like any help?' when you warmly mean it?
4. Can some be used with an uncountable noun? Give an example.

## Summary
• Some is usual in positive sentences. Any is usual in questions and negatives.
• Both can be used with plural countable nouns and with uncountable nouns.
• Offers often use some. 'Any key' can mean one of all the keys.

### Answers to practice
1. We have some paper, but we do not have any ink.
2. Are there any messages? Any correct question is acceptable.
3. Would you like some help?
4. Yes. There is some information on the page.

questions.question: Which noun is uncountable?
questions.explanation: We say a piece of information, not two informations.

questions.question: Which noun is countable?
questions.explanation: Messages can be counted: one message, two messages.

questions.question: Choose the correct phrase.
questions.explanation: Information is uncountable, so it takes much.

questions.question: How ____ computers are in the lab?
We do not have ____ time.
questions.explanation: Time as an amount is uncountable and the sentence is negative, so much fits.

questions.question: There are ____ pictures in this folder. The sentence is positive.
questions.explanation: Some is used in a positive sentence with a plural noun. A would need a singular noun.

questions.question: Are there ____ replies from the teacher?
Which sentence is a natural offer?
questions.explanation: Offers use some, and water is uncountable.

questions.question: 'Press any key' means
options: press one key, and it does not matter which approved key
questions.explanation: In this positive sentence, any means one out of the set.

questions.question: Write a negative sentence using any and the noun links.
questions.answer: We do not click any strange links.
questions.explanation: Any belongs in the negative sentence, and links is a plural countable noun.
